summary: LIGHT-TIME is a health monitoring system that constantly monitors astronauts' vitals. It identifies both current astronaut issues and illnesses (ex. heart attack) and can help predict future illnesses by using data taken from both earth and space human datasets. Our interface lets astronauts view their past and current vitals and will identify any data that is out of range, and suggest next steps.
details:
How does it work

LIGHT-TIME consists of 3 components, the suit, base station, and command center (Earth). To facilitate the flow of information the suit sends data to the base station and the base station forwards that data off to Earth. More specifically the suit sends one health “packet” a second to the base station allowing the crew to get alerts as abnormal conditions arise. A report to Earth arrives after a delay depending on the distance from Earth.

The skin suit constantly monitors the astronauts heart rate, blood oxygen, skin temperature, motion, muscle activity, and radiation exposure. LIGHT-TIME is able to identify any vitals that are out of range and identify if it's a sign of future illnesses and/or any health issues. As an added bonus, if something looks life threatening, the system will send out an alert to the other crew members alerting them of an astronaut in distress. This distress call would include the location and reason for the alert, but never any medical records of the patient. You may be wondering, “why is this important?” Well it’s important because in the vastness of space you may not always have a fellow crewmate nearby, and if/when something goes wrong you want to be sure that your crewmates will know where you are and come to your rescue. 

Since the data that the suit collects is sent to the base station it can check if there are any signs or trends towards a future illness (ex. Radiation poisoning, immune system decay, and heart disease). Helping to identify future space related illnesses prior to them occurring allows for treatment or proactive steps to be taken to reduce the risk of furthering illness. This is done with LIGHT-TIME by using fixed rules and simple statistics on every reading. 

The base station sends a package to Earth every 2 minutes, so that the flight surgeon on Earth can take a second look at what the data shows and what the base station recommended. The flight surgeon will either be happy that everything is going well and have no comments or be able to raise alerts that something is wrong. At the end of a day, there is also a summary that gets sent to Earth. A report also leaves the moment there is an early warning or an SOS. Every message arrives after the light time, stamped with when it left and the earliest a reply can come back. We hope that with more data and space travel the base stations will only need to send the daily summary to Earth.

The benefits

The crew gets a warning before an emergency, with time left before conditions become worse. For example, after six readings of falling blood oxygen levels, a warning will be sent to the user before an SOS call is made with a median lead time of ~97 seconds. When Earth is too far away to help in time, LIGHT-TIME triages and decides who can help. Upon enabling our trust rules we also found that false SOS alarm rates went from ~4 to none.

Health records stay private. Each crew member sees only their own data, the (CMO) and the flight surgeon can see everyone's, and an SOS shares only the who, what and where of the person in distress. These rules ensure that we keep data privacy as one of our highest priority while still saving lives.

Intended impact of the project

When on a space station, a crew can reach a flight surgeon in under a second. On the way to Mars a question takes at least 22 minutes for a round trip communication, that's not taking into account the time it takes for Earth to come up with an answer. 

NASA’s five hazards for space flight are: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and closed environments. LIGHT-TIME is built for that gap. It gives the CMO, who may not be a doctor, clear information including: how serious the reading is, how much time is left before conditions become worse, and whether Earth can answer first. It cuts false alarms so the crew trusts the ones that remain, and it sends Earth every report with its timing so nobody waits for a reply that could not have arrived. The same idea could help whenever help is far away and the link is slow, such as polar research stations or ships at sea.

Tools, coding languages, hardware, and software used to develop the project

Back end: Python, Flask, SQLAlchemy, SQLite and PostgreSQL, with 236 automated tests (pytest).

Front end: TypeScript, React and Next.js.
Hosting: Google Cloud Run at https://lighttime.health.
Suit design: an ESP32 microcontroller with MAX30102 (heart rate and blood oxygen), MAX30205 (skin temperature), MPU6050 (motion), MyoWare 2.0 (muscle) and SPACEDOS02 (radiation) sensors, plus a Bluetooth blood-pressure cuff.

In order to bring our product to life, we have designed a skinsuit that constantly monitors astronauts’ important vitals. The hardware includes a central microcontroller, a heart-rate + blood oxygen sensor (MAX30102) , a skin temperature sensor (MAX30205), a separate bluetooth enabled digital upper-arm cuff that will connect to the microcontroller wirelessly, a motion and activity sensor (MPU6050), a radiation exposure sensor (SPACEDOS02 ), and a muscle activation sensor.

The technical documentation on how this application functions and the designs behind the microcontroller and wiring can be found in the LightTime-Docs repository. (https://github.com/NASA-space-apps-the-procrastinators/LightTime-Docs).

Creativity

Instead of limiting ourselves to a system (or multiple systems) that already exist, we have decided to combine them into one piece of equipment that the astronauts would be able to wear. There’ll be no more need for daily checkins where astronauts get poked and prodded. With LIGHT-TIME this time can be instead taken to do a mental check in, and/or give the astronauts time to do literally anything else, like one more game of cards, a few more minutes of sleep, more time to talk with family, or just sit and relax. 

Having all the sensors on one piece of equipment allows for less cargo to be brought up into space and less components to go missing. It also allows for easier system integration, instead of a system trying to communicate with 5 or 6 different hardware systems that were made by different companies with different purposes, this system only needs to work with the technology it was built for. It allows for fewer devices and connections to manage as well as having easier documentation for how to fix something if anything goes wrong.

We have taken into consideration that the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) has developed a Bio-Monitor that has sensors on a skin suit. We are adding sensors to the skin suit which improves health information collection and LIGHT-TIME solves the delay of decision making from Earth when the delay is great enough. When LIGHT-TIME deems that the delay to Earth is too great it will suggest that the CMO take action instead of waiting for Earth’s reply.

Factors considered

We considered technology that already exists, instead of creating new everything, we build on the CSA Bio-Monitor smart shirt that already exists which limits costs, resources, weight and space it takes up on board.

With astronauts not necessarily being medical doctors, their understanding and analysis of all of their data can be confusing and misinterpreted. However, there would be a CMO who may be able to make sense of it all. Knowing this, our system identifies when something should be addressed right away (urgent, in red) and things that should be monitored (in orange).

A CSA staff member told us astronauts accept scheduled check-ups but do not want to be watched around the clock, and that health data must stay confidential. Given this feedback we decided to ensure that only full records go to the CMO and the flight surgeon, each crew member sees only their own data. Only the SOS is shared with everyone on board, only indicating who it is, where they are and what is the main issue (in case equipment is needed). We also acknowledge that there are moments where astronauts do not want to be monitored, so, we allow astronauts to take off the vest for a maximum of 5 hours a day (this would be something that can be changed as mission profiles differ). 

The same CSA staff member told us any AI must explain its recommendations and must not send health data to the open internet. LIGHT-TIME has fixed rules and simple statistics, every alert names the reading and the rule that raised it, and no language model or internet service is part of any medical decisions.

What's next for LIGHT-TIME

Not getting in the way. Monitoring must not distract the crew from the mission. LIGHT-TIME only alarms on readings it can trust, one bad reading can never raise an SOS, and slow drifts go into the daily summary.

Delay and blackouts. The ISS has near real time connectivity through relay satellites, the Moon is 1.3 seconds one-way, and Mars is 3 to 22 minutes one-way delay. While behind the Sun there is no link to Earth. The UI displays all these timing differences for convenience, and any messages that cannot leave wait in a queue until they can be sent.

Sudden events, not long illness. Astronauts are among the healthiest people there are, so we’ll set strong rules that watch for acute events such as falling blood oxygen levels.

An on-board medical reference. Using a combination of symptoms manually added and detected symptoms from the skin suit, LIGHT-TIME would scrape medical textbooks that were added pre-flight and matching of the symptoms in the textbook. It is a lookup, not a diagnosis, and the CMO would still decide the treatment plan.

Mood and vital signs together. In order to improve our health metrics we plan to link the mental-health check-ins to recorded sleep activity and heart-rate variability. This lets us flag mental-health as a potential health risk better using the coordinated data.

Privacy controls. To encourage privacy we would implement a privacy setting that stops health recording for a set amount of time. We would also implement an emergency unlock that lets a crewmate helping a casualty see that person's record. The emergency unlock would be logged and reviewed afterwards as this exposes confidential health information.

A real test. We would love to run a test in an analog habitat on Earth with an artificial delay imposed. This would allow us to see how astronauts and LIGHT-TIME function when they’re virtually on their own. The other benefit to a test like this is that we can test that the sensors are picking up all the data needed and not throwing false warnings or SOS signals. This test would also greatly further our rule definitions for alerting and perfect our “time left before conditions become worse” estimates.


NASA data used

LIGHT-TIME asks NASA JPL's Horizons system for the distance from Earth to Mars on the mission date and divides it by the speed of light. On 14 November 2026 Mars was about 198.1 million km away, so a message takes 660.86 seconds (11 minutes) one way and any reply needs 1,321.72 seconds (22 minutes) round trip. We check the figure against NASA's Deep Space Network Now feed, which shows the round-trip light time for spacecraft at Mars; on 15 November the two agreed to within 1.6 seconds. The Deep Space Network carries the signal, it does not set our number, and our figure leaves out time spent in relays and ground processing.
